title: VPIC Legislative Priorities and Annual Report Update
transcript: Order. First item on the agenda is agenda approval. Tim, Justin, anyone need to rearrange the order on this? No, Mr. Chair. Okay. I will look for a motion to approve the agenda. I'm going to be looking to Cam and Mike for a lot of these, I think. Cam, second by Mike. Assume the silence is good. So, a motion to approve the agenda. All in favor, please say aye. Aye. Any opposed? All right. Tim, Bill, Justin, any announcements or board members, any announcements? I'm another group of staff. Okay. So, next item on the agenda is the approval of the December minutes. I would entertain someone making a motion to approve the December 16, 2025 minutes. And Cam, and a second. Second. Perfect. Any corrections to those minutes? Hearing none. All those in favor of approving the December 16, 2025 minutes, please say aye. Aye. Any opposed? All right. I see no public on Zoom. Bill, it looks like you're in an empty room. That's correct, Mr. Chair. All right. And I think we can go ahead and turn it over to Eric and Tim for the VPIC presentation. Great, Mr. Chair. And I think we could turn it over to Eric for this that Eric had asked to come and talk to the board about what VPIC has in mind at the legislature this year. Some work we're doing on transition of OPEP funds for the state and teacher system. So with that, I'll turn it over to Eric. Thanks for being here today. Thank you all. Good morning. Happy New Year. Appreciate everybody's time this morning. A couple of things I wanted to update you all on. We did provide you with a copy of our annual report. We filed that to do January 15th in the legislature of every year. If you read through the executive summary there, you can see the high points from our year. Another strong year from an investment return standpoint. Another strong year for our private equity portfolio second year in a row that will rank number one in the country among large public pension funds. With regard to the OPEP legislation, we had a pretty thorough discussion at the December VPIC meeting and our supportive of the provisions in H567 that would make VPIC the fiduciary and trustee of those OPEP assets. Indeed, VPIC signed a more robust memorandum of agreement with the treasurer back in September that sort of contemplates this and ups the level of analysis and scrutiny that VPIC provides over those assets. Step one in that process is an asset liability study. We have kicked that process off with RVK. We expect to see preliminary results from the asset liability study in early February. We're working under two contracts with RVK at this point. Our VPIC has a contract with RVK as does the treasurer. So we're working through both of those contracts through that process. Once the purpose of the asset liability study is to strategically align those OPEP assets with the pension with the OPEP liabilities that they're set aside to fund. And that really starts with the actual or the valuations that SEAL does. We're working through that process now and we'll have an update for the treasurer's staff in the next few weeks. I would think when we see preliminary results. Following that, we would undertake a liquidity study to help us understand and help the treasurer understand the extent to which those OPEP portfolios could tolerate ill-liquid assets. As you add ill-liquid assets to a portfolio, you increase its expected return. You also increase its discount rate and the resulting liability decreases. So we think that's a good thing. Higher returns, lower liabilities. The challenge with ill-liquid assets is that there's a limit to how much each plan can tolerate in ill-liquid assets. Those plans need to have enough current liquid assets on hand to meet current obligations, whether for benefit payments or capital calls, without selling assets at discounted prices. So the liquidity study is a systematic and comprehensive exercise and modeling exercise to help us understand the extent to which those portfolios can tolerate ill-liquid assets. Once we have that in place, we would undertake a pacing study that helps us gauge how much a new ill-liquid assets, those funds should commit every year. That pacing study takes a look at the rate at which previous ill-liquid assets are drawing funds down. As you commit to an ill-liquid asset, it's not all invested at once. You're simply making a promise that over time, over a period called the investment period, is a general partner buys companies and invests in them. They'll call capital from the investors or the limited partners. As that's happening, older funds are returning capital as those portfolio companies are sold off or harvested. It's really a matter of kind of homing in on the strategic targets in those ill-liquid asset sections of the portfolio, knowing that money is coming and money is going to and from these funds. So with that in mind, the target of that is to have a pace of budget for ill-liquid asset commitments every year. That budget then is used to size new funds that are in the market. We have a robust underwriting process in place with our team and our consultant to make sure that to the extent ill-liquid funds are being considered, they're proving inconsistent with the goals of those portfolios and with the liabilities of those funds. And as we think about all this process in place currently with Treasury P-checks still being the fiduciary at every decision point along the way, whether it's finalizing strategic allocation or approving the pacing study or approving a commitment to a private equity fund, Mike, we would ask you to approve each recommendation as we move along. We share with you the analysis that's done to make sure you have a thorough understanding of what we're doing. An act of H567 would make VPIC the fiduciary and those decisions will be made side by side with the pension assets. Currently, we have four sleeves of pension assets, the three pension plans, as well as the teacher supplemental COLA plan. We would simply add the two additional sleeves, the teacher OPEB and the employee OPEB as additional sleeves to the VPIC platform. Then as future investment decisions are made, those two sleeves would share pro-rata or as appropriate in those new investment decisions going forward. If H567 is enacted, we would transfer the assets from the current platform over to VPIC. Liquid assets would be redeemed from the BlackRock index funds and deployed according to the new strategic targets by VPIC. And with regard to the illiquid assets, since they're not really redeemable, we would simply implement the legal documents to make VPIC the general, the limited partner versus a treasurer's office. So a lot of things happening there. But as you can see, it's a fairly robust and technical process that we go through with our consultants. We're at $8 billion in assets now. We could foresee being over $10 billion in the not too distant future with future OPEB contributions and future investment returns. Our current staffing level, we have four full-time employees. We think that presents some risks, especially with bringing on two new sleeves of assets. And we had a pretty robust conversation about staffing with VPIC at our last meeting. We are asking the legislature and we'll be testifying tomorrow morning that if H567 is enacted, we respectfully ask them to add a financial director, three-position to VPIC's compliment. Much of this comes from the Mercer compensation study that the legislature asked us to undertake in 22. That identified staffing as a significant investment risk. Since that time, we have added one position, but the fund has grown significantly in both sides and complexity. So we think it's time to add another position. We've not seen any real pushback from the administration on that position. However, they declined to put it in our requested budget. I've said a lot. Happy to take any questions. Take the discussion off in any direction you want to see fit. Any questions from board members? Sounds like you made it under 90 minutes, Eric. I'll give you all some time back. Thank you all. Thank you. All right. Tim, legislative update. Great. And I will be equally brief. This is. Thank you. Great. And I will be equally brief. This is.  is what we presented with the materials this month was 567, the bill that we have currently in the house. That bill has a number of components for the Treasurer's Office generally, but it has specifically to the board a few retirement related ones. Eric spoke in depth about what takes up the most real estate in the bill, which is the transfer of the investment fiduciary authority from the Treasurer to VPIC, that those sections also do some cleanup work where there was some language pertaining to investments that are still in the retirement statutes and the specific retirement system chapters. So there's just some geography work putting those into VPIC's chapter so that all of the relevant statutory authority is generally in one place. Another main piece of the retirement focused legislation is the pension funding task force. We talked about this a little bit before, I think in November or December, I provided a short memo overview. The idea with the task force is to focus solely on funding of the pension systems. Currently we have our 30 year closed amortization policies for the plans set forth in statute. And as we increase, particularly in the state and teacher system, as we get closer to the end date, the risk of volatility starts to curve up substantially. It's a little different on the, that volatility in the ADEC is still there for the municipal system, but because of our stated rate funding practices in practice, it's not felt as much because we don't pay the ADEC, whatever it is in this system, like we do the other two systems, but the policies out there. And so this task force, I think will inform Vemors, but it won't be as directly relevant to Vemors funding path as it is to the other two systems. But the goal is to look at this with a number of stakeholders and to kind of come back in advance of the next legislative session with some recommendations. And there are some neat things that our other systems are doing in that the Society of Actuaries has kind of vetted and recommends to mitigate your risk. So we'll be looking at those with stakeholders and coming back with some recommendations. Other sections, I think the only one that pertains directly to the municipal system is there is an option to purchase service for basically someone who serves as the president of an employee organization like NEA with full release from their service. So right now for the president of the NEA, I think it's a teacher who was in the teacher system, but if they go to serve in that role, they can't get any visitors credit because they're not teaching. This bill would allow that individual to purchase those years of service. And if they're in the teacher system, they'd purchase it from teachers, if they're in the municipal system, they'd purchase it from the municipal system. And it's really just to, it was put in after we had some discussions with NEA and realized that it could be a disincentive to younger folks to serve in those roles or to go for those roles. So it just adds one more basis for an individual to purchase service like Peace Corps, military, prior service, there's a number of reasons. And as we said, we really only expected to apply to one person and it would be actually really neutral. So no cost to the state. So those are the main substantive pieces in our legislative agenda this year. We are also requesting an additional position in the retirement division. When we look at our system, we are staffed, our member to staff ratio is over twice the median of peer systems. And so when you look at it against peers, you kind of think, okay, well, we're running pretty lean here. When I look at it from an actual workflow, I can tell you that we're running extremely lean and we've had a few new positions in recent years, but they are now fully roped into our daily work. And we still have some gaps that we need to fill, particularly with respect to oversight of the supplemental plans and our healthcare plans. So it's in those areas where we're really seeing the biggest need and value of an additional position in the retirement division. So that additional position is also in the legislative package. I think we're also submitting it in our budget request as well. We're having to answer any questions about that. One thing I will put for your consideration, both the state and the teachers board when looking at this, took up a motion to support the positions requested by VPIC and the retirement division. And I wanted to convey that to this board for your consideration. Do we want a motion for that? Morgan? I'm good with the motion for that. I like to make it. I move that VEMRS support the request for additional staff for VPIC and for the retirement division. Do we have a second? I'll second that. I'll second that. Any discussion on that motion? Tim, do you know how much money that is going to be? Would be? I don't have VPICs off hand. For ours, it would be approximately, I think we're factoring roughly $130,000 all in fully loaded with benefits. Thank you. I would expect that VPIC one to be a little bit above that. And I think I can't recall if Eric followed it to attention in this conversation, but similarly relative to peers in investment management and oversight in other statewide investment commissions, VPIC is sorely below the staffing levels that we would see among our peers. And I think Eric made reference to it, I just, in Tim noting the ratios being off, it is probably among our greater risks in the VPIC side of the staff to make sure that we're adequately staffed for the work that's happening. So. And Kim, I think from the comp studies that I've seen, I think even more so than the staffing ratios is the comp levels. So, I mean, they're kind of flip sides of the same coin, but in the investment staff, comp levels are pretty out of pace. 100%. And I think recognizing that staffing for these things are not as Vermont specific, probably as they might have been prior to COVID, they're not as Vermont specific in the risk of losing our staff and their opportunity to remain in Vermont and do their work elsewhere for other organizations. So, I think very much so, that's a both and from that comp study too. Thanks. I appreciate Veeamer's taking an action on this to endorse those positions on both fronts. Any other discussion on the motion? If not, we'll hold the vote on that. All those in favor of the motion to support the addition of those two positions in the budget, please say aye. Aye. Aye. Any opposed? Okay. Any other questions on the legislative update? Tim, I just have two quickies. You had sent out a drafting request with the packet. Did anything change between that and becoming an actual bill? Or anything substantive change that we know of? I don't believe so. Justin, any, I don't believe any changes have kind of hit at this point. Yep. Not that we've been told of, you know, who knows we're still early in the process, but I think that's still how it is right now. And at this point, just so you know where it is, Mike introduced it was at two weeks ago in the, in House GovOps and did a walkthrough of Senate GovOps too. So I think the two committee, main committees of jurisdiction have had a walkthrough. Okay. Perfect. All right. Anything that you want to add to the legislative update, Tim? No, that's all for me. I mean, we'll see where it goes. It's early. Yeah. I mean, the fact that they're taking testimony at this early is a good sign, but yeah, things do change there for the next few months. So keep us posted on that. That brings us to the end of our agenda. Tim or Justin, any other business you have for the board? I did just want to give you a heads up about some work we're doing on the state side. As you know, the state is the fiduciary for the 457.  plan, but we do have municipal members in that plan. We have had an expense account due because of the fee structure way back when before we switched to Prudential. So this is in the 20 teens. We had substantial excess funds in a plan expense account that we were we've been using to wind down to subsidize the cost to members. And we've now exhausted that. We still have enough for a while about a year probably, but we have been working on the state side to get the plans to basically so that like all the other plans, members are paying the cost of the of the plan because we don't have any other revenues to fund those plans from. So it was about half the cost that we've been using this to subsidize the member fees. And so we've been providing some analysis to the state board and they're looking at it. I think we're hoping to make a decision in the February meeting and then have it implemented in the summer. But I just wanted to give you a heads up about it because it does it will affect municipal employees who are participating in the state's 457 plan. So just, you know, if anyone asks you about it, I wanted you to have some awareness of it. We've had robust analysis from Sarah at RBK kind of helping the board think through, you know, whether it's a per head fee, whether it's an increased asset fee, what do we do to make it equitable, perhaps some caps, ceilings, sorry floors or ceilings that fees are applied to. So they're looking at all that right now. And we're talking to Empower to make sure that structurally everything, you know, they agree with how we're seeing the world. So just wanted to let you know that that work is happening over there. And we will let you know what the result is. Sounds good. Any questions on that? Oops. All right. I believe we are together again, February 17th. Sounds right. Enjoy the rest of your January. And I will entertain a motion to adjourn. To see Kim and a second by John and a third by Mike. All those in favor, please say aye. And we adjourn. Thanks all. Take care, folks. Promise to a short one, Morgan. Bye.
summary:
### **Final Meeting Summary**

#### **1. Approval of Minutes & Agenda**
- Approved December meeting minutes.
- Agenda approved for discussion.

#### **2. VPIC Annual Report & OPEP Legislation (H567)**
- **VPIC’s Performance:**
  - Strong investment returns.
  - Top-ranked private equity portfolio.
- **OPEP Legislation (H567):**
  - VPIC supports making VPIC the fiduciary of OPEP assets.
  - New memorandum of agreement signed with the treasurer.
  - Asset-liability study initiated with RVK (preliminary results expected early February).
  - Goal: Align OPEP assets with liabilities using SEAL valuations.

#### **3. Asset-Liability & Liquidity Studies**
- **Valuations:**
  - SEAL conducting valuations (updates expected soon).
- **Liquidity Study:**
  - Assess illiquid asset tolerance while balancing returns and liquidity needs.
- **Pacing Study:**
  - Determine annual commitments to illiquid assets (considering capital calls and returns).
- **Next Steps:**
  - Recommendations shared with the treasurer for approval.
  - Current fiduciary process involves Treasury P-checks.
  - If H567 passes, VPIC would assume fiduciary role.

#### **4. Impact of H567 (Fiduciary Transfer & Expansion)**
- **Current Structure:**
  - Four pension sleeves (three pension plans + teacher supplemental COLA).
- **Proposed Changes:**
  - Adding two more sleeves (teacher OPEB & employee OPEB) to VPIC’s platform.
- **Asset Transfer:**
  - Liquid assets redeployed; illiquid assets transferred via legal adjustments.
- **Growth & Risks:**
  - Current assets: **$8B** (expected to exceed **$10B**).
  - Current staffing (4 FTEs) may be insufficient for new responsibilities.
- **Staffing Request:**
  - Proposed **3-position financial director** addition (based on Mercer study) pending administration approval.
- **Legislative Update:**
  - H567 progressing in the House; retirement provisions discussed in depth.

#### **5. Retirement Legislation & Task Force Updates**
- **Transfer of Investment Fiduciary Authority:**
  - Bill transfers authority from the Treasurer to VPIC.
  - Cleanup work to consolidate investment-related language into VPIC’s chapter.
- **Pension Funding Task Force:**
  - Focus on 30-year closed amortization policies and volatility risks.
  - Gather stakeholder input; recommendations before next legislative session.
- **Service Purchase Option:**
  - Bill includes option for individuals serving as president of an employee organization (e.g., NEA) to purchase service credit.

#### **6. Staffing Requests & Budget Approval**
- **Volunteer Programs (VPIC):**
  - Requested one additional position to address staffing gaps (included in legislative package and budget request).
- **Retirement Division:**
  - Requested one additional position due to high member-to-staff ratio (over twice the median of peer systems).
  - Estimated cost: **~$130,000** (fully loaded with benefits).
- **Motion Approved:**
  - Unanimous support for staffing requests based on peer comparisons and risk mitigation.

#### **7. Compensation Study & Legislative Updates**
- **Compensation Concerns:**
  - Investment staff compensation **100% out of pace**.
  - Post-COVID staffing challenges increase turnover risk.
- **Motion Approved:**
  - Unanimous support for adding two positions to the budget.
- **Legislative Update (457 Plan):**
  - Bill introduced two weeks ago; walkthroughs in relevant committees (no substantive changes yet).
  - State managing 457 plan; excess funds exhausted.
  - Decision on fee structure (per-head vs. asset-based fees) expected in February, implementation by summer.
  - RBK (Sarah) assisting with analysis; discussions with Empower ongoing.

#### **8. Next Meeting**
- Scheduled for **February 17th**.

---
**Summary compiled in a professional, structured format for clarity and action tracking.**
